name: NihongoHub Japan Prefecture Dataset
description: All 47 Japanese prefectures for travelers and Japanese learners: signature and lesser-known foods, cultural sights, sub-areas, and a 5-axis profile (food/culture/city/access/nature). Each food and culture entry carries the public source it was drawn from. The nature score is derived from GBIF biodiversity occurrence data.
license: Facts are free to cite and reuse. Attribution to NihongoHub (https://www.nihongo-hub.com) is requested. Each item also carries its own upstream source.

prefectures.name: Hokkaido
prefectures.summary: Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost and largest prefecture centered on Sapporo, offers winter powder snow and onsen resorts alongside summer lavender fields and rolling farmland. It is known for cold-water seafood including uni and crab, Ainu cultural heritage around Lake Akan, and the Otaru Canal, a preserved 19th-century waterway lined with stone warehouses.

prefectures.name: Aomori
prefectures.summary: Honshu's northernmost prefecture, Aomori is Japan's apple kingdom (about 60% of national output) and home to the thunderous Nebuta Festival, with Hirosaki Castle ranking among the country's top cherry-blossom spots.

prefectures.name: Iwate
prefectures.summary: Iwate is Japan's second-largest prefecture, in northern Tohoku, blending the UNESCO World Heritage temples and Pure Land gardens of Hiraizumi with the rugged, ria-indented Sanriku coast and its seafood-rich waters. Its castle-town capital Morioka was named one of The New York Times' "52 Places to Go in 2023."

areas.note: Sanriku coast city famed for Jodogahama Beach, a white-rock shoreline with rocky islets and Blue Cave (Aonodokutsu) boat cruises.

prefectures.name: Miyagi
prefectures.summary: Miyagi, in Japan's Tohoku region, is famed for Matsushima Bay—one of the "Three Most Scenic Spots of Japan," with around 260 pine-clad islets—and for its lively capital Sendai, the "City of Trees" known for grilled beef tongue (gyutan) and the giant paper-streamer Tanabata festival each August.

foods.name: Matsushima oysters (松島の牡蠣)
foods.note: Plump oysters from Matsushima Bay, a winter delicacy celebrated at the February Oyster Festival and eaten grilled, fried (kaki fry) or raw.

culture.name: Matsushima Bay (松島)
culture.note: One of the 'Three Views of Japan', with around 260 pine-clad islands; ~1 hour from Sendai, reachable by sightseeing cruise.

areas.name: 仙台市

prefectures.name: Akita
prefectures.summary: Akita is a snowy northern Tohoku prefecture famed for its Kanto Festival of giant lantern-laden bamboo poles balanced on performers' bodies, top-grade sake and rice, and Lake Tazawa, Japan's deepest lake. It is also home to the namahage demon-visitor tradition and beautifully preserved Edo-period samurai townscapes.

prefectures.name: Yamagata
prefectures.summary: Yamagata, in the Tohoku region facing the Sea of Japan, grows about 70% of Japan's cherries and is home to the cliffside mountain temple Yamadera (Risshakuji). In winter, Mount Zao's fir trees freeze into famous "snow monsters" (juhyo) above its onsen ski slopes.

prefectures.name: Fukushima
prefectures.summary: Tohoku's largest prefecture by area, Fukushima pairs the samurai history and lacquerware of the Aizu highlands with Pacific coastline, and is split into three distinct regions: mountainous Aizu, central Nakadori, and coastal Hamadori. It is known for hilltop castles, hot-spring resorts, and dramatic scenic rail like the Tadami Line.

prefectures.name: Ibaraki
prefectures.summary: Ibaraki, on the Pacific coast northeast of Tokyo, is famed for Hitachi Seaside Park's springtime hills of blue nemophila and autumn red kochia, and for Kairakuen in Mito, one of Japan's "Three Great Gardens" with around 3,000 plum trees. It's also home to Tsukuba Science City, a hub of national research institutions.

foods.note: Ibaraki's most iconic food: small-bean fermented soybeans from Mito, prized for strong stickiness, rich aroma and umami. Eaten over rice, on toast or in pasta.

prefectures.summary: A landlocked, mountainous prefecture in northern Kanto famous for its hot springs, including Kusatsu Onsen, which boasts the largest natural hot-water output in Japan. It is also home to the UNESCO World Heritage Tomioka Silk Mill and the birthplace of the daruma doll.

foods.name: Mizusawa Udon / Himokawa Udon
foods.note: Gunma is a major wheat region; Mizusawa udon (regarded as one of Japan's top-quality noodles, smooth with a firm bite) and ultra-wide himokawa udon are signatur

foods.name: Yakimanju (grilled miso buns)
foods.note: Steamed buns skewered, grilled and coated in a sweet miso glaze. A beloved Edo-period street snack originating in Maebashi, with a festival in Isesaki.

foods.name: Konnyaku
foods.note: Gunma grows over 90% of Japan's konjac taro, making this low-calorie, vegan-friendly jelly food a defining local product.

foods.name: Okkirikomi
foods.note: A rustic home-style stew of wide flat noodles simmered with seasonal vegetables in soy-based broth; a Gunma B-class winter comfort dish, less known to overseas

foods.name: Tomioka Horumon-age
foods.note: Despite the name suggesting fried offal, Tomioka's specialty horumon-age is actually breaded, skewered and fried chikuwa fish cake. A quirky local-only snack.

culture.name: Tomioka Silk Mill
culture.note: UNESCO World Heritage site (2014), Japan's first modern silk-reeling factory (est. 1872) blending Western and Japanese architecture; demonstrations and live sil

culture.name: Kusatsu Onsen (Yubatake)
culture.note: One of Japan's top three hot-spring resorts with the country's highest natural spring output; the steaming Yubatake source and yumomi water-stirring song-and-da

culture.name: Ikaho Onsen 365 Stone Steps
culture.note: A 300m-plus historic stone staircase (365 steps) lined with craft shops and inns, famed for retro charm and iron-rich 'golden' brown waters.

culture.name: Takasaki Daruma painting workshop (Daimonya)
culture.note: Takasaki produces ~80% of Japan's daruma dolls; at Daimonya, a fourth-generation craftsman lets visitors learn the history and paint their own daruma.

culture.name: Konnyaku Park (make-your-own konjac)
culture.note: A free-admission factory park where visitors see how konnyaku is produced and try a hands-on konjac-making experience, plus a buffet of konnyaku dishes.

areas.name: 草津
areas.note: Home to Kusatsu Onsen, one of Japan's top three hot springs, centered on the steaming Yubatake hot-water field.

areas.name: 高崎
areas.note: The birthplace of the daruma doll and a gateway city near the World Heritage Tomioka Silk Mill.

areas.name: 前橋
areas.note: The prefectural capital, offering rose gardens, Tone River cycling paths, and access to Mt. Akagi.

prefectures.name: Saitama
prefectures.summary: A landlocked prefecture just north of Tokyo, Saitama is best known for Kawagoe's "Little Edo" warehouse townscape and the mountainous Chichibu region's gorges, shrines, and hot springs. Omiya, its urban core, hosts the Railway Museum and a historic bonsai village.

foods.name: Soka senbei (grilled soy-sauce rice crackers)
foods.note: Hard-baked rice crackers from Soka, dating to the Edo period when Soka was a post town on the Nikko Kaido highway; pressed flat with an oshigawara press for a c

foods.name: Unagi kabayaki (grilled eel, Urawa/Kawagoe)
foods.note: Eel split, deboned, skewered and grilled in a sweet soy-sauce marinade; a ~200-year-old tradition kept alive around Urawa, where it has long been a valued prote

foods.name: Saitama udon
foods.note: Saitama is Japan's second-largest udon producer (after Kagawa) thanks to its wheat output, with many local variations served across the prefecture.

foods.name: Chichibu miso potato (miso poteto)
foods.note: Battered fried potato chunks topped with sweet miso sauce; originated as a farm-worker snack in the Chichibu mountains using locally grown potatoes cooked over

foods.name: Kawahaba udon (Konosu)
foods.note: An extra-wide, flat udon inspired by the breadth of the Arakawa river; one of Saitama's distinctive regional udon variants and a lesser-known local specialty.

culture.name: Kawagoe 'Little Edo' (Koedo) Kurazukuri Street & Toki no Kane bell tower
culture.note: Historic warehouse-lined streets preserved from the Edo period, with the landmark Toki no Kane bell tower that still rings four times daily.

culture.name: Kawagoe Hikawa Shrine
culture.note: Roughly 1,500-year-old shrine famous as a matchmaking 'power spot'; its summer 'Enmusubi Furin' festival hangs around 2,100 Edo-style wind chimes across the gro

culture.name: Mitsumine Shrine, Chichibu
culture.note: Mountain shrine at ~1,100 m altitude enshrining wolves as divine messengers; regarded as one of the Kanto region's top spiritual power spots.

culture.name: Omiya Bonsai Village & Bonsai Art Museum
culture.note: Cluster of historic bonsai nurseries founded in 1925 after the Great Kanto Earthquake; nurseries welcome visitors free, and the city art museum (reopened March

culture.name: Nagatoro river boating & Iwadatami rocks (kotatsu boats in winter)
culture.note: Pole-steered wooden boats glide past the Iwadatami rock formation, a designated Cultural Landscape of Japan; in winter you can ride heated kotatsu boats on the

areas.name: 川越
areas.note: "Little Edo" town with preserved kura-zukuri clay storehouses and the Toki no Kane bell tower, ~30 min from central Tokyo.

areas.name: 秩父
areas.note: Mountain gateway with scenic gorges, Mitsumine Shrine, hot springs, and a long textile-weaving tradition.

areas.name: 大宮
areas.note: Commercial hub of Saitama City with a major shinkansen station, the Railway Museum, and the Omiya Bonsai Village.

prefectures.name: Chiba
prefectures.summary: Chiba is Japan's eastern gateway, home to Narita International Airport and, in Urayasu, the Tokyo Disney Resort, while its Boso Peninsula offers ocean views, surf beaches and the cliffside "Hell Lookout" of Mount Nokogiri.

foods.name: Peanuts (Chiba rakkasei)
foods.note: Chiba produces the vast majority of Japan's peanuts; eaten boiled, roasted, sugared, or in miso. A signature regional souvenir.

foods.name: Namero (fish tartare)
foods.note: A Boso Peninsula fisherman's dish of chopped/pounded mackerel or horse mackerel seasoned with ginger and miso.

foods.name: Choshi seafood / kaisendon
foods.note: Choshi has been Japan's top fishing port by volume for years thanks to converging warm/cold currents; fresh sashimi bowls and seasonal catch are a draw.

foods.name: Katsuura Tantanmen
foods.note: A spicy soy-and-chili-oil ramen with minced pork and onion, invented in Katsuura in the 1950s to warm fishermen; 30+ accredited shops each do their own version.

foods.name: Kujukuri sesame sardines (goma-iwashi)
foods.note: Sun-dried sardines from the Kujukuri/Boso coast seasoned with mirin and dusted in black sesame; a lesser-known local preserved-fish specialty.

culture.name: Naritasan Shinshoji Temple
culture.note: 1,000+ year-old temple near Narita Airport drawing over 10 million visitors a year; goma fire rituals, an Important Cultural Property pagoda, and a lively Omote

culture.name: Mount Nokogiri & Nihonji Temple
culture.note: 329m 'Sawtooth Mountain' with one of Japan's largest stone Buddhas, over 1,500 arhat statues, and the cliff-edge 'Jigoku Nozoki' (View of Hell) lookout.

culture.name: Inubosaki Lighthouse, Choshi
culture.note: An 1874 British-designed brick lighthouse at the easternmost cape of the Kanto region, a Registered Tangible Cultural Property and listed among Japan's top ligh

culture.name: Choshi Electric Railway (Choden)
culture.note: A tiny 6.4km line famous for self-deprecating humor and 'nure senbei' wet rice crackers; stations sell family-made snacks and a Nauru friendship pavilion opened

culture.name: Chikura flower fields & hana ryori, southern Boso
culture.note: A 'village of flowers' where farmers grow edible blooms from January to March, served as flower-based cuisine (hana ryori); a low-profile seasonal experience.

areas.name: 成田市
areas.note: Site of Narita International Airport and Naritasan Shinshoji, a Shingon Buddhist temple founded in 940 and one of Japan's most-visited New Year's pilgrimage spots.

areas.name: 浦安市
areas.note: Home of Tokyo Disney Resort (Disneyland and DisneySea), the first Disney park built outside the United States.

areas.name: 鴨川市
areas.note: Pacific-coast town on the Boso Peninsula known for Kamogawa Sea World aquarium and ocean scenery.

prefectures.name: Tokyo
prefectures.summary: Tokyo, Japan's capital, spreads across 23 central wards and blends neon nightlife with calm temple gardens and famously punctual transport. Landmarks include Sensō-ji, the city's oldest temple, entered through the Kaminarimon gate in Asakusa, and Meiji Jingū, a shrine set in a Harajuku forest, while the Yanaka district preserves old-town shitamachi streets.

foods.name: Monjayaki (Tsukishima Monja Street)
foods.note: Tokyo's signature shitamachi (old downtown) dish: a runny flour batter with cabbage and toppings cooked by diners on a tabletop griddle. Tsukishima Monja Street

foods.name: Edomae sushi
foods.note: Tokyo (old Edo) is the birthplace of nigiri 'Edomae' sushi using Tokyo Bay seafood; the official Tokyo guide profiles it among the city's defining local foods.

foods.name: Tokyo ramen (Tokyo Ramen Street)
foods.note: Soy-based 'Tokyo-style' ramen is a city staple; Tokyo Ramen Street beside Tokyo Station gathers eight acclaimed shops, each with its own variation.

foods.name: Omoide Yokocho yakitori alleys (Shinjuku)
foods.note: Narrow, smoky postwar lanes near Shinjuku Station packed with tiny grilled-chicken-skewer counters; a nostalgic, local-favorite alternative to polished restaura

foods.name: Himitsudo ningyo-yaki, Azabu-Juban
foods.note: Handmade ningyo-yaki (little filled sponge cakes) from a long-running wagashi shop along the cobblestone Azabu-Juban shopping street, away from the main tourist

foods.name: Togoshi Ginza shopping street snacks
foods.note: A 1.3 km local shopping street with around 400 shops and cheap street snacks, far quieter and cheaper than central Tokyo districts.

culture.name: Sensoji Temple & Nakamise, Asakusa
culture.note: Tokyo's oldest temple (founded 7th century), entered through the Kaminarimon Thunder Gate and the bustling Nakamise shopping street; the city's most-visited tem

culture.name: Meiji Jingu (Meiji Shrine), Harajuku/Yoyogi
culture.note: Shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set in a 700,000-plus square-meter man-made forest; receives around 3 million worshippers over New Year, t

culture.name: Yanaka & Nezu old-town district
culture.note: Surviving shitamachi area with Yanaka Ginza shopping street, the historic Yanaka Cemetery, and Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest shrines famous for its spring

culture.name: Nezu Shrine azalea garden
culture.note: One of Tokyo's oldest shrines, with tunnel-like vermilion torii gates and a spring (April-early May) Azalea Festival of thousands of blooms - a quieter alternat

culture.name: SCAI The Bathhouse, Yanaka
culture.note: A 200-year-old former public bathhouse converted into a contemporary art gallery showing Japanese avant-garde and international artists - culture inside a prese

culture.name: HAGISO, Yanaka
culture.note: A renovated old wooden apartment turned cafe-and-gallery cultural complex, a hub of the Yanesen creative scene off the standard tourist path.

prefectures.name: Kanagawa
prefectures.summary: Just south of Tokyo, Kanagawa pairs the international port city of Yokohama with the temple-filled former capital of Kamakura and the volcanic hot-spring resorts of Hakone. It's an easy day-trip prefecture combining harbor skylines, the open-air Great Buddha, and seaside island views.

foods.name: Yokohama Chinatown (nikuman & shumai)
foods.note: Japan's largest Chinatown; famous for pork buns (nikuman) and steamed shumai dumplings, plus a local Chinese-influenced ramen called sanma-men.

foods.name: Shirasu-don (Shonan whitebait bowl)
foods.note: A Kamakura/Shonan signature: soft, slightly salty whitebait served over rice. Raw nama-shirasu is only available the day it is caught.

foods.name: Yokosuka Navy Curry
foods.note: Hearty curry based on a recipe adopted by the former Imperial Japanese Navy from British beef stew; a defining dish of the port city Yokosuka.

foods.name: Misaki maguro (tuna), Miura Peninsula
foods.note: Misaki Port at the tip of the Miura Peninsula is a quiet fishing town renowned for tuna; restaurants serve unusual cuts like maguro kabuto-yaki (grilled tuna he

foods.name: Odawara kamaboko (fish cake)
foods.note: A lesser-known craft specialty: pink-and-white steamed fish cake said to have been refined in Odawara around 220 years ago.

culture.name: Great Buddha of Kamakura (Kotoku-in)
culture.note: 13th-century bronze Daibutsu, one of Japan's largest; visitors can step inside the hollow statue.

culture.name: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine
culture.note: Kamakura's most important Shinto shrine, founded 1063, dedicated to Hachiman and central to the city's samurai history.

culture.name: Hakone Shrine (Lake Ashinoko torii)
culture.note: Lakeside shrine at the foot of Mt. Hakone, famous for its red torii gate standing in Lake Ashinoko.

culture.name: Samukawa Shrine
culture.note: A serene shrine with roughly 1,600 years of history, rarely visited by overseas tourists, traditionally revered for warding off misfortune.

culture.name: Koganecho, Yokohama (art district)
culture.note: A former red-light area beneath the train tracks reborn as an artist community with galleries and studios; an offbeat cultural walk.

areas.name: 横浜市
areas.note: Kanagawa's largest city and a historic port; sightseeing centers on the Minato Mirai waterfront with museums and harbor views.

areas.name: 鎌倉市
areas.note: Japan's political capital during the Kamakura period (1185-1333); home to the open-air bronze Great Buddha at Kotoku-in.

areas.name: 江の島
areas.note: Small offshore island known for Enoshima Shrine, the Iwaya caves, and shirasu (baby-sardine) rice bowls with ocean views.

prefectures.name: Niigata
prefectures.summary: Facing the Sea of Japan, Niigata is Japan's rice and sake heartland, prized for premium Koshihikari rice, dozens of sake breweries, and abundant seafood. In winter its mountains receive some of the country's heaviest, powdery snowfall, drawing skiers and onsen-goers to the legendary "Snow Country."

foods.name: Koshihikari rice & local sake
foods.note: Niigata is Japan's top rice region (prized Koshihikari) and has the most sake breweries in the country; rice and sake are its signature pairing.

foods.name: Wappameshi
foods.note: Premium Niigata rice steamed in a cylindrical cedar 'wappa' box, topped with seasonal mountain and sea ingredients such as salmon, oysters or chicken.

foods.name: Noppe (noppei-jiru)
foods.note: A homestyle simmered vegetable dish (konjac, carrot, lotus root, shiitake, sometimes salmon roe) that locals eat at festivals and New Year; little known outside

foods.name: Suruten (squid 'tempura')
foods.note: A Joetsu-area specialty: squid salted overnight, then shredded and deep-fried, giving a deeper flavor than ordinary squid tempura.

culture.name: Bandai Bridge (Bandaibashi)
culture.note: Landmark stone-arch bridge over the Shinano River, Japan's longest river, designated an Important Cultural Property and the symbol of central Niigata City.

culture.name: Northern Culture Museum (Hoppo Bunka Hakubutsukan)
culture.note: Preserved mansion and gardens of the wealthy Ito landowner family of Echigo, with art and architecture showcasing Niigata's rural traditions; famous for its gia

culture.name: Yahiko Shrine
culture.note: Ancient and revered Shinto shrine at the foot of Mt. Yahiko, popular for its spiritual significance combined with natural scenery and seasonal foliage.

culture.name: Furumachi Geigi (geisha) experience
culture.note: Niigata's 200-year-old geisha district, ranked historically with Kyoto's Gion and Tokyo's Shinbashi; ryotei welcome first-time visitors and offer programs to wa

culture.name: Sado Island taiko with Kodo
culture.note: On Sado Island, the Sado Island Taiko Centre run by the world-renowned ensemble Kodo lets visitors try Japanese drumming; Kodo also hosts the annual Earth Celeb

areas.name: 新潟市
areas.note: The prefectural capital and a port city on the Sea of Japan, about 2 hours from Tokyo by Joetsu Shinkansen; known for sake, seafood, and a historic geisha district.

areas.name: 佐渡島
areas.note: Japan's sixth-largest island, reached by ferry from Niigata; famed for the Sado gold mine, Kodo taiko drumming and the Earth Celebration festival, and terraced rice paddies.

areas.name: 越後湯沢
areas.note: Snow Country resort town in Yuzawa, ~75-90 min from Tokyo by Shinkansen; a cluster of ski resorts and 800-year-old hot springs, the setting of Kawabata's novel 'Snow Country'.

prefectures.name: Toyama
prefectures.summary: Toyama sits between the soaring 3,000-meter peaks of the Northern Japan Alps and the deep, seafood-rich waters of Toyama Bay, and is best known for the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, where spring snow walls tower up to roughly 20 meters. It also offers UNESCO World Heritage gassho-zukuri villages at Gokayama and renowned coastal hot springs facing the Tateyama mountains.

foods.name: Shiroebi (white shrimp / glass shrimp)
foods.note: Called the 'Jewel of Toyama Bay'; Toyama Bay is essentially the only place it is caught commercially. Served as sashimi, sushi or kakiage tempura, prized for it

foods.name: Hotaru-ika (firefly squid)
foods.note: The 'Mystery of Toyama Bay' - tiny squid that glow blue-white, caught mainly off Namerikawa in spring. Classic local preparation is with vinegared miso (sumiso)

foods.name: Masuzushi (pressed trout sushi)
foods.note: Edo-period local specialty: salt-pickled trout fillet pressed over rice and wrapped in bamboo leaf in a round box. A famous Toyama station bento / souvenir.

foods.name: Toyama Black Ramen (Toyama Black)
foods.note: Lesser-known regional ramen born postwar in Toyama City to feed laborers - very dark, salty soy-sauce tare over thick curly noodles, balanced with a lighter bro

foods.name: Himi udon (and Himi Banya-gai port market)
foods.note: Off-the-beaten-path Himi City specialty - hand-pulled, oil-free elastic udon counted among Japan's top udon styles; eat it at the Himi Banya-gai fishing-port ma

culture.name: Kurobe Dam
culture.note: Japan's tallest arch dam (186m), completed 1963. The thunderous water discharge (late June to mid-October), ~10 tons/second, is the signature spectacle viewed f

culture.name: Gokayama Gassho-zukuri Villages (Ainokura & Suganuma)
culture.note: UNESCO World Heritage (1995) thatched-roof gassho-zukuri villages in Nanto City; you can stay overnight in a family-run heritage farmhouse and dine around the i

culture.name: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route Snow Corridor (Yuki-no-Otani)
culture.note: Mountain-crossing route across the North Japan Alps famed for ~14-18m snow walls at Murodo (2,450m); the Snow Wall Walk runs roughly mid-April to late June each

culture.name: Inami woodcarving town (Yokamachi Street, Nanto City)
culture.note: Japan's top woodcarving town with ~100 master artisans; the workshop-lined street is like an open-air museum, and you can book a hands-on carving experience (e.

culture.name: Gokayama washi papermaking experience
culture.note: Hands-on traditional washi paper craft going back 1,200+ years; make your own postcards, bookmarks or fans, with English-friendly classes near the Gokayama vill

areas.name: 富山市
areas.note: Prefectural capital and the Toyama-side gateway to the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route.

areas.name: 高岡市
areas.note: Historic metalworking city home to a Great Buddha and the access point for the Gokayama gassho-zukuri villages.

areas.name: 氷見市
areas.note: Coastal town famed for Toyama Bay seafood, Himi beef, and hot springs with views of the Tateyama Range across the water.

prefectures.name: Ishikawa
prefectures.summary: Ishikawa stretches along the Sea of Japan, anchored by the castle town of Kanazawa with its celebrated Kenrokuen, one of Japan's three great gardens, and preserved geisha and samurai districts. North of the city, the rugged Noto Peninsula offers dramatic coastal scenery, centuries-old lacquerware crafts, and seafood markets.

foods.name: Kaisendon / Omicho Market seafood (snow crab, nodoguro, amaebi)
foods.note: Ishikawa sits where warm and cold Sea of Japan currents meet, giving exceptional seafood; Omicho Market is the 'Kitchen of Kanazawa' with 180+ shops. Winter bri

foods.name: Jibuni (duck and vegetable stew)
foods.note: A Kanazawa signature: duck (sometimes other poultry) coated in flour and simmered with seasonal vegetables in dashi, giving a characteristically thick, glossy b

foods.name: Noto beef (Noto-gyu)
foods.note: Wagyu from black cattle raised on the Noto Peninsula; production is so small it is rarely shipped outside Ishikawa, making it a true local-only delicacy compare

culture.name: Kenrokuen Garden
culture.note: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens, beside Kanazawa Castle. Its name means 'garden of six attributes' (spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, water, and

culture.name: Higashi Chaya District
culture.note: Kanazawa's largest preserved teahouse (chaya) district, with wooden-latticed geisha houses, gold-leaf shops, and traditional cafes along narrow lanes.

culture.name: Nagamachi Samurai District
culture.note: Preserved former samurai residential quarter with earthen walls and lanes; some old residences are open to visitors, others now host cafes and craft shops.

culture.name: Gold leaf (kinpaku) workshop in Higashi Chaya
culture.note: Kanazawa produces almost all of Japan's gold leaf. Visitors can hand-apply gold leaf to chopsticks, plates, or boxes using artisan tools (e.g. sunago-zutsu) in

culture.name: Noto Peninsula farmhouse stays and Shiroyone Senmaida rice terraces
culture.note: Family-run farmhouse inns let visitors join seasonal rice planting and support recovery after the 2024 Noto earthquake; the Shiroyone Senmaida terraced rice fie

areas.name: 金沢
areas.note: Prefectural capital known for Kenrokuen garden, the Higashi Chaya geisha district, and Omicho seafood market.

areas.name: 輪島
areas.note: Noto Peninsula town famed for over 500 years of Wajima-nuri lacquerware and its lively morning market.

areas.name: 見附島
areas.note: Uninhabited rock islet off Suzu nicknamed 'Battleship Island,' rising roughly 28 meters from the sea and popular for sunrises.

prefectures.name: Fukui
prefectures.summary: Fukui is Japan's "Dinosaur Kingdom," home to the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum and roughly 80% of the country's dinosaur fossil finds. It also draws visitors to the dramatic Sea of Japan rock pillars of Tojinbo and the serene Soto Zen training temple Eiheiji.

foods.name: Echizen Crab (Echizen-gani)
foods.note: Premium male snow crab landed on the Echizen coast, tagged with a yellow port label for authenticity. Season opens Nov 6; a signature winter delicacy at local r

foods.name: Echizen Oroshi Soba
foods.note: Classic northern Fukui dish: cold buckwheat noodles topped with grated daikon, bonito flakes and green onion. Gained fame after Emperor Showa praised it in 1947

foods.name: Sauce Katsudon

foods.name: Habutae Mochi
foods.note: Silky-smooth steamed rice-flour confection named after Fukui's glossy Habutae silk; a lesser-known elegant local sweet and souvenir.

foods.name: Aburaage (fried tofu) at Taniguchiya
foods.note: Fukui City has topped Japan in per-capita aburaage consumption for decades and is home to Japan's only aburaage-focused restaurant, Taniguchiya - an offbeat loc

culture.name: Eiheiji Temple
culture.note: One of two head temples of Soto Zen Buddhism; a 70-building mountain complex with 200+ resident monks and nuns, Japan's largest Zen training site.

culture.name: Tojinbo Cliffs
culture.note: Over a kilometer of dramatic columnar basalt cliffs along the Sea of Japan; a 'Top 100 Japanese Sunset' spot, best seen by boat tour at sunset.

culture.name: Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum
culture.note: One of the world's top dinosaur museums and Japan's largest, with 50 skeletons including local Fukuiraptor and Fukuisaurus plus animatronic dinosaurs.

culture.name: Ichijodani Asakura Clan Ruins & Family Site Museum
culture.note: Excavated Sengoku-era castle town once home to 10,000+ people, with a full-scale reproduction of a samurai street and the Asakura mansion; quiet and atmospheric

culture.name: Echizen Washi Village (papermaking)
culture.note: Birthplace of 1,500-year-old Echizen washi paper (once used for banknotes); hands-on papermaking workshops at the source village.

areas.name: 勝山市
areas.note: Home of the world-class Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum and Japan's most prolific fossil excavation site.

areas.name: 坂井市
areas.note: Site of the Tojinbo cliffs, rare columnar basalt rising up to ~25m over the Sea of Japan, near Mikuni Port.

areas.name: 福井市
areas.note: The prefectural capital and gateway, with Ichijodani Asakura clan ruins and access to nearby Eiheiji Zen temple.

prefectures.name: Yamanashi
prefectures.summary: Landlocked Yamanashi sits in the shadow of Mount Fuji, sharing Japan's tallest, most iconic peak with neighboring Shizuoka and cradling the scenic Fuji Five Lakes. It is also Japan's leading wine region, with over 80 wineries centered on the native Koshu grape, plus orchards famed for peaches and grapes.

foods.name: Houtou (ほうとう)
foods.note: Yamanashi's signature comfort dish: flat, wide wheat noodles simmered in a rich miso broth with kabocha pumpkin and seasonal vegetables, served in an iron pot.

foods.name: Koshu wine (甲州ワイン)
foods.note: Made from the indigenous Koshu grape; Yamanashi has 90+ wineries producing roughly 30% of Japan's wine, with the Koshu Valley around Katsunuma/Koshu City a popu

foods.name: Shingen mochi & Yamanashi fruit (peaches, grapes)

foods.name: Kofu tori motsuni (甲府鳥もつ煮)
foods.note: Local Kofu specialty of chicken giblets simmered fast over high heat with sugar and soy sauce until glossy and caramelized, giving a salty-sweet glaze. A B-grad

foods.name: Ozara (おざら)
foods.note: A chilled-noodle cousin of houtou: the same wide wheat noodles served cool with a warm dipping broth, a homestyle dish rarely featured in tourist guides.

culture.name: Chureito Pagoda / Arakura Fuji Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida)
culture.note: Five-storied pagoda above Fujiyoshida reached by ~400 steps, offering the iconic framed view of Mount Fuji; spectacular with cherry blossoms in mid-April and au

culture.name: Kuonji Temple, Minobusan (身延山久遠寺)
culture.note: Head temple of the Nichiren sect of Buddhism; visitors climb 287 steep stone steps (or take a ropeway) past gates, pagodas and a treasure hall on a sacred mount

culture.name: Koshu Valley wineries (Katsunuma/Koshu City)
culture.note: Japan's historic wine capital with 90+ wineries open for tastings amid vineyards, an easy day trip from Tokyo and the cultural heart of Japanese winemaking.

culture.name: Nishijima washi papermaking (西嶋和紙の里)
culture.note: The village of Nishijima has deep ties to traditional washi paper; at Nishijima Washi no Sato visitors can try hands-on papermaking workshops, a craft tradition

areas.name: 甲府市
areas.note: Prefectural capital in a mountain-ringed basin, gateway to Shosenkyo Gorge and a historic samurai (Takeda) town.

areas.name: 富士吉田市
areas.note: Base town for climbing Mount Fuji and home to the iconic Arakurayama Sengen Park five-storied pagoda view.

areas.name: 甲州市
areas.note: Contains the Katsunuma district, the birthplace of Japanese winemaking with dozens of clustered wineries.

prefectures.name: Nagano
prefectures.summary: A landlocked, mountainous prefecture in central Japan ringed by the soaring peaks of the Japanese Alps, Nagano hosted the 1998 Winter Olympics and draws visitors with ski resorts, historic temples and the wild snow monkeys that bathe in steaming hot springs at Jigokudani.

foods.name: Gohei mochi
foods.note: Pounded rice shaped onto a flat skewer, coated in a sweet-savory walnut/sesame miso sauce and grilled; a hearty central-mountain Nagano street food.

culture.name: Jigokudani Yaen-Koen (Snow Monkey Park)
culture.note: The world's only spot where wild Japanese macaques bathe in natural hot springs, set in a steaming valley at ~850m elevation snow-covered much of the year.

areas.name: 長野市
areas.note: Prefectural capital and home to Zenko-ji, a 7th-century Buddhist temple whose main hall is a National Treasure.

areas.name: 松本市
areas.note: Site of Matsumoto Castle, one of Japan's twelve original surviving keeps and a National Treasure, set against the Northern Alps.

areas.name: 軽井沢町
areas.note: Highland resort town about an hour from Tokyo, known for cool summers, forest villas and a large outlet shopping plaza.

prefectures.name: Gifu
prefectures.summary: A landlocked, mountainous prefecture in central Japan famed for the UNESCO World Heritage gassho-zukuri thatched farmhouses of Shirakawa-go and the well-preserved Edo-era streets of Takayama in the Japan Alps. It also boasts Gero, counted among Japan's three great hot-spring resorts.

foods.name: Hoba miso

foods.name: Takayama ramen
foods.note: Takayama's soul-food ramen: thin curly noodles in a simple soy-based broth, distinct from richer styles elsewhere.

culture.name: Gujo Hachiman castle town
culture.note: The 'City of Water' near the Nagara River, with samurai-style Yanagimachi houses, craftsman lanes and clear canals running past old homes.

culture.note: UNESCO-recognized traditional Japanese paper with 1,300+ years of history; visitors can try hand-papermaking at the Mino washi museum in the Mino area.

areas.name: 高山市
areas.note: Old castle town with beautifully preserved Edo-period streets (Sanmachi) and daily morning markets.

areas.name: 白川郷
areas.note: UNESCO World Heritage village of steep thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses, stunning under winter snow.

areas.name: 郡上八幡
areas.note: Riverside castle town known for crystal-clear waterways and the summer Gujo Odori dance festival.

prefectures.name: Shizuoka
prefectures.summary: Shizuoka is famed for sweeping views of Mount Fuji and produces a large share of Japan's green tea, while its Izu Peninsula draws visitors to coastal hot springs and fresh seafood.

foods.name: Shizuoka green tea (cha / matcha)
foods.note: Shizuoka produces roughly 40% of all Japanese green tea, the single largest output of any prefecture; pristine slopes and water make for high-quality leaves.

foods.name: Wasabi-zuke (sake-lees pickled wasabi)
foods.note: A traditional Shizuoka preserve using the whole wasabi root pickled in sake lees; rare and expensive outside the prefecture, pairs well with drinks and rice.

culture.name: Mount Fuji (Shizuoka side)

culture.name: Miho no Matsubara & Nihondaira

culture.name: Oigawa Railway steam locomotive (Kawane)
culture.note: The only railway in Japan running steam locomotives year-round, with engines dating to the 1930s, threading the scenic, off-the-beaten-path Oigawa River valley.

areas.name: 静岡市
areas.note: The prefectural capital, gateway to tea fields and Suruga Bay seafood.

areas.name: 浜松市
areas.note: The prefecture's most populous city, known for Lake Hamana and as a musical-instrument manufacturing hub.

areas.name: 熱海市
areas.note: A classic seaside hot-spring resort on the Izu Peninsula, close to Tokyo by Shinkansen.

prefectures.name: Aichi
prefectures.summary: Aichi, centered on Japan's fourth-largest city Nagoya, is the heartland of the auto industry (home to Toyota) and home to feudal landmarks like Nagoya Castle and the ancient Atsuta Shrine. Its Mikawa Bay coast offers small islands and the original wooden keep of Inuyama Castle, one of Japan's oldest.

foods.name: Gamagori udon (蒲郡うどん)

foods.name: Toyohashi Inari udon (豊橋カレーうどん style / Inari udon)

culture.name: Nagoya Castle (名古屋城)

culture.name: Atsuta Jingu / Atsuta Shrine (熱田神宮)

culture.name: Inuyama Castle (犬山城)
culture.note: Japan's oldest existing wooden castle keep, a designated National Treasure perched above the Kiso River, with a historic castle town below.

areas.name: 名古屋

areas.name: 犬山
areas.note: Castle town in northern Aichi with Inuyama Castle, one of Japan's oldest original wooden keeps and a National Treasure.

areas.name: 竹島

prefectures.name: Mie
prefectures.summary: Mie is home to Ise Jingu, Japan's most sacred Shinto shrine complex of 125 shrines, and the Ise-Shima coast where Mikimoto produced the world's first cultured pearl in 1893. Its indented Pacific bays are dotted with islands and worked by ama, the traditional free-diving women who harvest abalone and shellfish.

foods.name: Ise udon
foods.note: Distinctively thick, soft noodles served with only a small amount of dark, sweet soy-based tare; historically an easy-to-digest meal for Ise Shrine pilgrims.

culture.name: Ise Jingu (Ise Grand Shrine)
culture.note: Japan's most sacred Shinto shrine complex of 125 shrines, centered on the Naiku (Inner) and Geku (Outer) shrines dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu.

culture.name: Meoto Iwa (Wedded Rocks), Futami
culture.note: Two sea rocks joined by a heavy shimenawa sacred rope off Futami Okitama Shrine; a symbol of marital harmony, with sunrise framed between them from May to July.

culture.name: Okage Yokocho, Ise
culture.note: Edo-style market street near Ise Jingu's Naiku recreating the golden age of pilgrim culture, lined with food stalls and shops (home of Akafuku mochi).

areas.name: 伊勢
areas.note: Site of Ise Jingu, Japan's most revered Shinto shrine, plus the lively Okage Yokocho old-town streets.

areas.name: 鳥羽
areas.note: Birthplace of cultured pearls (Mikimoto Pearl Island) and a hub for ama diver culture and the aquarium.

areas.name: 答志島
areas.note: Largest of Toba's four inhabited islands; a working fishing community reached by ferry with abundant fresh seafood.

prefectures.name: Shiga
prefectures.summary: Shiga wraps around Lake Biwa, Japan's largest freshwater lake and one of the oldest in the world, ringed by a roughly 200 km cycling route. The prefecture pairs the lake's island shrines and boat cruises with Edo-era castle towns and merchant canals just a short train ride from Kyoto.

areas.name: 竹生島
areas.note: Sacred island in northern Lake Biwa with Hogon-ji temple and Tsukubusuma Shrine, reached by boat.

prefectures.name: Kyoto
prefectures.summary: Kyoto, the imperial capital from 794 to 1868, keeps feudal history visible on nearly every street, anchored by temples like Fushimi Inari Taisha with its thousands of vermilion torii gates and the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji). The Arashiyama bamboo grove and the historic geisha district of Gion reflect its role as Japan's cultural heart, home to delicate, seasonal Kyo-ryori cuisine.

foods.name: Nishin soba (herring soba)

culture.note: A gold-leaf-covered Zen pavilion reflected in its mirror pond; one of Kyoto's most photographed sights. Open 9am-5pm, entrance ~500 yen.

prefectures.name: Osaka
prefectures.summary: Osaka, Japan's food capital and home to the neon Dōtonbori entertainment district, centers on street-food culture and historic landmarks including Osaka Castle, originally built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 16th century. The city serves as a transport hub under an hour from Kyoto, Nara, and Kobe, with a distinctive Kansai dialect and cuisine of takoyaki, okonomiyaki, and kushikatsu.

prefectures.name: Hyogo
prefectures.summary: Hyogo stretches from the cosmopolitan port city of Kobe (home of world-famous Kobe beef) to the National Treasure Himeji Castle, Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage site. The prefecture reaches the Seto Inland Sea via Awaji Island, linked to the mainland by the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge.

areas.note: Largest island in the Seto Inland Sea, reached by the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge and known for the Naruto whirlpools.

prefectures.name: Nara
prefectures.summary: Nara was Japan's first permanent capital (710-784) and holds more UNESCO World Heritage sites than any other prefecture, where ancient temples, free-roaming sacred deer, and mountainsides of cherry blossoms meet. This landlocked Kansai prefecture is a living museum of the country's earliest court culture.

foods.name: Miwa Somen
foods.note: Japan's oldest hand-stretched thin wheat noodles, with over 1,200 years of history in the Miwa district of Sakurai City; prized for a chewy yet smooth texture.

foods.note: A Nara specialty since the 8th-century Heijo-kyo capital era, made by repeatedly marinating gourd, cucumber, ginger and other vegetables in sake lees.

areas.note: The capital city, home to Nara Park with over 1,000 free-roaming sika deer, plus the great bronze Buddha at Todaiji and Kasuga Taisha shrine.

areas.name: 吉野町
areas.note: Mount Yoshino is renowned for roughly 30,000 cherry trees in about 200 varieties and is part of the UNESCO-listed Sacred Sites of the Kii Mountain Range.

areas.name: 斑鳩町
areas.note: Site of Horyuji, founded in 607, whose halls are among the world's oldest surviving wooden structures and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

prefectures.name: Wakayama
prefectures.summary: Wakayama, on the Kii Peninsula south of Osaka, is Japan's spiritual heartland: it holds the Buddhist monastery town of Koyasan and the ancient Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trails, both part of the UNESCO World Heritage "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range." Its rugged coastline adds hot-spring resorts, white-sand beaches, and Nachi Falls, Japan's tallest waterfall at 133 meters.

culture.name: Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes & Kumano Sanzan
culture.note: Ancient UNESCO-listed pilgrimage trails linking the three Kumano grand shrines (Hongu Taisha, Hayatama Taisha, Nachi Taisha) through the Kii mountains.

culture.name: Nachi Falls & Seiganto-ji Pagoda

areas.name: 和歌山市
areas.note: Prefectural capital and gateway, home to hilltop Wakayama Castle and the ferry port for Tomogashima.

areas.name: 白浜町
areas.note: Seaside hot-spring resort with a 500-meter white-sand beach and Adventure World safari-aquarium park.

areas.name: 友ヶ島
areas.note: Uninhabited islands off Wakayama City in the Kitan Strait, known for moss-covered Meiji-era fort ruins resembling Studio Ghibli's Laputa.

prefectures.name: Tottori
prefectures.summary: Tottori is Japan's least-populous prefecture, hugging the Sea of Japan coast in the Chugoku region and famous above all for the Tottori Sand Dunes, a 16-km sweep of golden coastal dunes where you can ride camels or sandboard. Beyond the sand it offers a rugged volcanic peak (Mount Daisen), yokai folklore, and quiet seaside towns.

areas.name: 鳥取市
areas.note: The capital city, gateway to the Tottori Sand Dunes (Tottori Sakyu) and the Sand Museum's seasonal sculpture exhibits.

areas.name: 境港市
areas.note: Birthplace of manga artist Mizuki Shigeru; Mizuki Shigeru Road is lined with bronze statues of yokai from 'GeGeGe no Kitaro'.

areas.name: 倉吉市
areas.note: Home to the Shirakabe Dozo-gun, a preserved district of white-plastered, red-tiled-roof storehouses dating from the Edo period.

prefectures.name: Shimane
prefectures.summary: Shimane, on Japan's San'in coast facing the Sea of Japan, is the mythic "Land of the Gods," home to Izumo Taisha, one of the country's oldest and most revered Shinto shrines. It also holds the National Treasure Matsue Castle, the UNESCO World Heritage Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine, and the volcanic Oki Islands.

foods.name: Shijimi clams (宍道湖のしじみ)

foods.note: Luxury white-fleshed fish landed on the Sea of Japan coast around Matsue and Izumo; served grilled, as sashimi, or over rice as a premium local lunch.

foods.name: Hekayaki (へか焼き)
foods.note: An Oda City specialty hotpot/sukiyaki simmered with tilefish (amadai) and nodoguro; a regional B-class gourmet dish rarely found elsewhere.

areas.name: 出雲市
areas.note: Home to Izumo Taisha, one of Japan's oldest Shinto shrines, dedicated to the deity of relationships.

areas.name: 松江市
areas.note: The castle town capital, with the National Treasure Matsue Castle and the top-ranked Adachi Museum of Art garden nearby.

areas.name: 隠岐諸島
areas.note: A UNESCO Global Geopark of volcanic islands in the Sea of Japan, known for dramatic sea cliffs and outdoor activities.

prefectures.name: Okayama
prefectures.summary: Okayama, one of Japan's sunniest prefectures, is home to Korakuen, one of the country's three great landscape gardens, sitting beside the black-walled Okayama Castle. It is also famed for the thousand-year-old unglazed Bizen pottery tradition.

foods.name: Momotaro peaches & Muscat grapes (Fruit Kingdom)
foods.note: Okayama is known as Japan's 'Fruit Kingdom,' prized for white Momotaro peaches and seedless Muscat of Alexandria grapes; eaten fresh or in cafe parfaits.

foods.name: Demi-katsudon (demi-glace pork cutlet bowl)
foods.note: An Okayama City B-class specialty: breaded pork cutlet over rice topped with rich demi-glace sauce instead of the usual egg.

foods.name: Hinase kakioko (oyster okonomiyaki)
foods.note: Savory okonomiyaki packed with freshly harvested oysters from the Hinase fishing town in Bizen City; originated in the 1960s using surplus oysters.

foods.name: Tsuyama horumon udon (offal udon)

foods.name: Hiruzen yakisoba
foods.note: Highland specialty from the Hiruzen plateau: chicken and cabbage yakisoba in a sweet-and-spicy miso-based sauce; a regional dish few overseas visitors know.

culture.name: Korakuen Garden
culture.note: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens, built 1687-1700 by lord Ikeda Tsunamasa; lawns, ponds, tea/rice fields with seasonal blossoms and illumination events.

culture.name: Okayama Castle (Ujo / 'Crow Castle')
culture.note: Black-lacquered keep first built 1597 in Azuchi-Momoyama style, reconstructed 1966; pairs with adjacent Korakuen via a combined ticket.

culture.name: Kurashiki Bikan Historical Quarter
culture.note: Edo-era canal district of white-walled warehouses, museums and cafes; canal boat tours are a signature experience.

culture.name: Bizen ware pottery-making
culture.note: 1,000-year-old unglazed, high-fired stoneware; visitors can throw their own piece at the Bizen pottery studio in Ujo Park near Okayama Castle.

areas.name: 岡山市
areas.note: Prefectural capital, home to Korakuen Garden and the black Okayama Castle (Ujo).

areas.name: 倉敷市
areas.note: Edo-era canal town whose Bikan Historical Quarter preserves white-walled merchant storehouses.

areas.name: 犬島
areas.note: Small Seto Inland Sea art island (Okayama City) with the Seirensho Art Museum built into a former copper smelter.

prefectures.name: Hiroshima
prefectures.summary: Hiroshima is home to two UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Atomic Bomb Dome and Peace Memorial Park, which tell the story of August 1945 and the global call for peace, and the vermilion "floating" torii gate of Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima Island. The prefecture also offers Seto Inland Sea scenery, fresh oysters, and the island-hopping Shimanami Kaido cycling route.

areas.name: 広島市
areas.note: Prefectural capital with the Atomic Bomb Dome, Peace Memorial Park and Museum, and Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki.

areas.name: 宮島
areas.note: Sacred island (formally Itsukushima) famed for the over-water Itsukushima Shrine and its iconic floating torii gate, plus Mount Misen and free-roaming deer.

areas.name: 尾道市
areas.note: Hillside port town of temples and cats; gateway to the 70 km Shimanami Kaido cycling route linking islands across the Seto Inland Sea to Shikoku.

prefectures.name: Yamaguchi
prefectures.summary: Yamaguchi, at the western tip of Honshu, is famed as the "fugu (pufferfish) capital of Japan" via the port of Shimonoseki and for picture-perfect scenery like the azure waters around Tsunoshima and the 123 vermilion torii of Motonosumi Inari Shrine. It also holds the elegant wooden arches of Iwakuni's Kintaikyo Bridge and the Edo-era castle town of Hagi.

foods.note: Pressed, layered sushi with colorful toppings (egg, sakura denbu, shiitake, local renkon lotus root); said to date back 300+ years as samurai battle provisions.

foods.note: A celebrated Iwakuni City specialty lotus root, prized for its crunch and used in local sushi and dishes; less known to foreign visitors than fugu.

foods.name: Ayu (sweetfish) caught by cormorant fishing
foods.note: Freshwater sweetfish caught traditionally by cormorant fishing on the Nishiki River, named for its melon/cucumber-like fragrance; a regional seasonal delicacy.

culture.name: Kintaikyo Bridge (Iwakuni)
culture.note: Five-arch wooden bridge first built in 1673 over the Nishiki River; iconic in cherry-blossom and autumn-foliage seasons.

culture.name: Akiyoshido Cave & Akiyoshidai Plateau (Mine)
culture.note: Japan's largest limestone cave (~9-11 km total, ~1 km public walking course) beneath Akiyoshidai National Park; famed 'Hundred Plates' terraced formation.

culture.name: Hagi castle town
culture.note: One of Japan's best-preserved samurai castle towns and home of Hagi-yaki pottery; named a New York Times travel destination for 2024.

culture.note: Hands-on Hagi-yaki ceramics workshops in Hagi; the soft-textured ware famously changes color with use and is prized for tea ceremony.

areas.name: 下関市
areas.note: Strait-side port city known as the fugu (pufferfish) capital of Japan.

areas.name: 角島
areas.note: Island reached by the scenic Tsunoshima Ohashi bridge over turquoise waters.

areas.name: 岩国市
areas.note: Home to the five-arched wooden Kintaikyo Bridge, one of Japan's most famous bridges.

prefectures.name: Tokushima
prefectures.summary: Tokushima, on the eastern side of Shikoku, is famous for the 400-year-old Awa Odori summer dance festival and the powerful Naruto whirlpools in the strait facing Awaji Island. Its mountainous interior hides the remote Iya Valley and its thrilling vine suspension bridges.

foods.note: Naruto Kintoki sweet potatoes are prized for natural sweetness; Naruto-dai (sea bream) grows firm-textured in the strait's fast currents.

foods.name: Iya Soba
foods.note: Rustic mountain buckwheat noodles made with no binding agent, giving a rough texture and short, thick strands; served in the remote Iya Valley.

culture.note: Remote Iya hamlet where 350+ life-size handmade scarecrows by artist Tsukimi Ayano outnumber living residents; a surreal monument to rural depopulation.

areas.name: 三好市
areas.note: Gateway to the secluded Iya Valley and its Iya no Kazurabashi vine suspension bridge.

prefectures.name: Kagawa
prefectures.summary: Japan's smallest prefecture punches far above its size: it's nicknamed "Udon Prefecture" for its chewy Sanuki udon served at hundreds of shops, and its capital fronts the island-dotted Seto Inland Sea, gateway to world-famous contemporary-art islands.

areas.note: The second-largest island in the Seto Inland Sea, known as Japan's 'Olive Island' and for the tidal sandbar Angel Road.

prefectures.name: Ehime
prefectures.summary: Ehime, on the northwest coast of Shikoku facing the Seto Inland Sea, is famed for Dogo Onsen, one of Japan's oldest hot springs with over 1,000 years of recorded history, and for the citrus-growing islands linked by the Shimanami Kaido cycling route. Its mild climate, feudal-era Matsuyama Castle, and mikan (mandarin orange) orchards make it a relaxed gateway to island-hopping.

areas.note: Seto Inland Sea island with the Murakami Kaizoku (pirate) Museum and Mt. Kiro viewpoints.

prefectures.name: Kochi
prefectures.summary: Kochi sprawls across the wild Pacific-facing south of Shikoku, famed for the dam-free Shimanto River (Japan's "last clear stream"), seared bonito (katsuo no tataki), and links to samurai reformer Sakamoto Ryoma. Rugged capes and clear waters reward travelers who venture off the beaten path.

foods.name: Katsuo no tataki (straw-seared bonito)
foods.note: Kochi's signature soul food: skin-on bonito flame-seared over burning rice straw (warayaki), sliced thick, and eaten with salt or ponzu plus garlic/ginger/onion

foods.name: Sawachi ryori (large-platter feast)
foods.note: A celebratory style of serving sashimi, sushi, grilled fish and seasonal delicacies arranged together on one large ~36-39cm platter, traditionally for weddings

foods.name: Hirome Market dining
foods.note: Lively indoor food hall in Kochi City with ~60 stalls and communal seating where you sample katsuo no tataki and local dishes amid Kochi's famous 'okyaku' drink

foods.name: Utsubo (moray eel)
foods.note: A lesser-known Kochi delicacy: despite its fierce look, moray eel has delicate, collagen-rich white flesh, served deep-fried (kara-age), as tataki, or in fish-p

foods.name: Susaki nabeyaki ramen
foods.note: A local soul-food noodle from Susaki City served boiling-hot in an enamel pot (originated 1940s for delivery so it wouldn't cool), topped with chicken, egg and

culture.name: Kochi Castle
culture.note: One of only 12 Japanese castles retaining its original Edo-period keep, and the only one keeping both the original tower and Honmaru Palace; 360-degree views ov

culture.name: Katsurahama Beach & Sakamoto Ryoma area
culture.note: Iconic scenic beach with a famous statue and memorial museum to hometown hero Sakamoto Ryoma, plus the Katsurahama Aquarium in the surrounding park.

culture.name: Yosakoi Festival (August)
culture.note: Kochi City's signature summer festival: ~190 teams and ~18,000 dancers blend the traditional naruko-clapper Yosakoi dance with modern music across the city; 202

culture.name: Chikurin-ji Temple
culture.note: ~1,300-year-old temple (No. 31 on the Shikoku 88-temple pilgrimage) with a five-story pagoda and gardens; its Main Hall is a nationally designated Important Cul

culture.name: Niyodo River canyoning / packrafting (Niyodogawa)
culture.note: Guided adventure tours through the limestone gorges and hidden waterfalls of the famously clear 'Niyodo Blue' river, with gear and English-speaking guides avail

areas.name: 高知市
areas.note: Prefectural capital; home to Kochi Castle and the lively Hirome Market for fresh katsuo no tataki.

areas.name: 四万十市
areas.note: Gateway to the Shimanto River, prized for its railless 'chinkabashi' submersible bridges and clear-stream canoeing.

areas.name: 沖の島
areas.note: Remote island off Sukumo City with stone-walled terraced villages and the Pacific's southernmost Shikoku waters.

prefectures.name: Fukuoka
prefectures.summary: Fukuoka is Kyushu's largest and most vibrant prefecture, famous for Hakata ramen, lively yatai (open-air food stalls) along Hakata Bay, and as a gateway to Asia just a short ferry ride from South Korea. It blends a buzzing modern city with castle towns and easy day-trip islands.

foods.name: Hakata Ramen (tonkotsu)
foods.note: Fukuoka's signature ramen: ultra-rich, milky pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth simmered for hours with thin, straight noodles; born in the Hakata district and served a

foods.name: Motsunabe (offal hot pot)
foods.note: A local hot pot of beef or pork tripe with cabbage, garlic chives and chili in a soy- or miso-based broth, cooked at the table; a Fukuoka winter favorite.

foods.name: Hakata Udon (gobo-ten udon)
foods.note: Lesser-known to foreigners but said to have origins in Hakata: soft, springy noodles in a clear niboshi-katsuobushi-kombu broth, often topped with burdock tempu

foods.name: Yanagawa Unagi no Seiro-mushi (steamed eel over rice)
foods.note: In the canal town of Yanagawa, freshwater eel is steamed over rice in a wooden box so the rice absorbs the eel's flavor; a regional dish many city visitors miss

culture.name: Dazaifu Tenmangu Shrine
culture.note: Head of ~12,000 Tenjin shrines and dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, deity of learning; famous for thousands of plum trees that bloom in February and an iconi

culture.name: Kushida Shrine
culture.note: Founded in 757 AD in central Hakata; the spiritual home of the July Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival with its towering, racing floats.

culture.name: Nanzoin Temple Reclining Buddha (Sasaguri)
culture.note: Mountain temple ~21 min by JR from Hakata, home to the world's largest bronze reclining Buddha (41 m long, 300 tons); part of the Sasaguri 88-temple pilgrimage.

culture.name: Nokonoshima Island Park
culture.note: A short ferry from Fukuoka city; a flower park with seasonal cosmos, cherry blossoms and rapeseed against sea views, a quiet alternative to the city crowds.

areas.name: 福岡市
areas.note: The prefectural capital and Kyushu's biggest city; home to Hakata Station, Hakata Bay, and the famous yatai food stalls.

areas.name: 北九州市
areas.note: Northern industrial city on the Kammon Straits, home to Kokura Castle, the only standing castle keep in the prefecture.

areas.name: 能古島
areas.note: Small island in Hakata Bay, about a 10-minute ferry from Meinohama, known for its flower park and autumn cosmos fields.

prefectures.name: Saga
prefectures.summary: Saga Prefecture is the birthplace of Japanese porcelain, home to the famed Arita, Imari and Karatsu pottery towns whose blue-and-white wares were exported to Europe for over 400 years. It also boasts the vast Yoshinogari Yayoi-period ruins and Yobuko's lively morning squid market.

foods.name: Saga beef (Saga-gyu)
foods.note: Premium Wagyu raised exclusively in Saga, prized for fine marbling and melt-in-the-mouth texture; served as steak, sukiyaki or shabu-shabu.

foods.name: Ureshino tea (Ureshino-cha)
foods.note: Distinctive curled-leaf green tea grown in the Ureshino basin for ~500 years, with rich aroma and a bittersweet profile.

foods.name: Sicilian rice (Shishirian raisu)
foods.note: Quirky Saga City yoshoku dish created around 1977: rice topped with sauteed meat, fresh salad and mayonnaise. Local comfort food rarely found elsewhere.

foods.name: Onsen yudofu (hot-spring tofu)
foods.note: Ureshino specialty where local alkaline sodium-bicarbonate spring water dissolves the tofu into a silky, milky, sweet texture; a vegetarian-friendly regional di

culture.name: Yutoku Inari Shrine
culture.note: One of Japan's three great Inari shrines; vermilion halls built on tall stilts into a hillside (nicknamed the Nikko of the West), drawing ~3 million visitors a

culture.name: Yoshinogari Historical Park
culture.note: 73.7-hectare reconstruction of one of Japan's largest Yayoi-period settlements, with watchtowers, dwellings and excavated relics.

culture.name: Arita (Arita-yaki porcelain town)
culture.note: Birthplace of Japanese porcelain (production since 1616); a main street lined with galleries and working kilns where you can watch artisans and buy directly.

culture.name: Okawachiyama (Village of Secret Kilns), Imari
culture.note: Former Nabeshima-clan secret kiln village (1675-1871) tucked into steep mountains; chimney smoke and a hidden-village atmosphere across the seasons.

culture.name: Tenchadai 'Heavenly Tea Table', Ureshino
culture.note: Outdoor tea experience at 200m elevation in the Soejimaen tea fields, where growers brew and serve their own tea surrounded by sweeping tea-plant and mountain v

areas.name: 有田町
areas.note: Birthplace of Japanese porcelain; spring Arita Ceramic Fair and kiln tours.

areas.name: 唐津市
areas.note: Coastal town with hilltop Karatsu Castle and the November Karatsu Kunchi float festival.

areas.name: 高島
areas.note: Small 'cat island' off Karatsu with the lottery-luck Hoto Shrine, about 10 minutes by boat.

prefectures.name: Nagasaki
prefectures.summary: Nagasaki was Japan's main window to the outside world during the Edo-era isolation, and its hilly harbor city blends Dutch, Chinese and Christian heritage with sobering atomic-bomb memorials. The prefecture also encompasses 594 islands, the most of any in Japan, scattered with hidden-Christian churches and uncrowded beaches.

foods.name: Nagasaki Champon (ちゃんぽん)
foods.note: Hearty noodle soup in a creamy pork/chicken broth loaded with seafood, pork and vegetables, created at the Chinese restaurant Shikairou in the late Meiji era. N

foods.name: Sara Udon (皿うどん)
foods.note: A 'plate noodle' relative of champon: crispy fried thin noodles (or soft thick noodles) topped with a thickened seafood-and-vegetable gravy. A Nagasaki staple a

foods.name: Castella (カステラ)
foods.note: Moist honey sponge cake brought by Portuguese traders in the 16th century and adapted in Nagasaki; long-running maker Fukusaya dates to 1624.

foods.name: Goto Udon & 'jigoku-daki' (五島うどん／地獄炊き)
foods.note: Thin, springy udon from the Goto Islands with reportedly 1,000+ years of history (counted among Japan's great udon). Eaten 'jigoku-daki' style: boiled in an iro

foods.name: Casdoce / Kasudosu (カスドース) of Hirado
foods.note: A 400-year-old Hirado confection: castella dipped in egg yolk and fried in sugar syrup. Once a treat reserved for the Hirado feudal lords during the era of nati

culture.name: Glover Garden (グラバー園)
culture.note: Hillside open-air museum of nine Western-style residences (1860s-1910s) above Nagasaki Port, centered on the 1863 former Glover Residence (Japan's oldest surviv

culture.name: Oura Church (大浦天主堂)
culture.note: Built in 1865, Japan's oldest existing Christian church and a National Treasure, dedicated to the 26 Martyrs of Nagasaki; a component of the 'Hidden Christian S

culture.name: Gunkanjima / Hashima Island (軍艦島・端島)
culture.note: Abandoned former coal-mining island ~20 km off Nagasaki Port, once among the world's most densely populated places; visited only via authorized boat tours. UNES

culture.name: Hidden Christian villages of Sotome – Shitsu & Ono Churches (外海 出津・大野教会堂)
culture.note: Quiet coastal villages where 'Kakure Kirishitan' secretly kept their faith; Fr. de Rotz's stone Shitsu and Ono churches survive on hills overlooking the Goto-na

culture.name: Kuroshima Church & the Goto island churches (黒島天主堂・五島の教会群)
culture.note: Remote-island Romanesque churches built by descendants of hidden Christians using local Kuroshima granite and Arita-porcelain floor tiles; an off-the-beaten-pat

areas.name: 長崎市
areas.note: The harbor capital: Peace Park and Atomic Bomb Museum, the reconstructed Dejima trading post, Glover Garden, and the Mount Inasa night view.

areas.name: 五島列島
areas.note: Western archipelago of around 150 islands dotted with hidden-Christian churches (UNESCO-listed sites) and Takahama Beach, rated among Japan's most beautiful.

areas.name: 対馬
areas.note: Mountainous border island near Korea, prized by hikers and birdwatchers and home to the rare Tsushima leopard cat (Tsushima yamaneko).

prefectures.name: Kumamoto
prefectures.summary: Kumamoto is a Kyushu prefecture defined by dramatic nature and history: the imposing reconstructed Kumamoto Castle, one of Japan's three great castles, and Mount Aso, which holds one of the world's largest active volcanic calderas. Its coast trails off into the Amakusa islands, home to UNESCO-listed Hidden Christian sites and fresh seafood.

foods.name: Basashi (horse meat sashimi)
foods.note: Kumamoto's signature delicacy; thinly sliced raw horse meat served with grated garlic/ginger and soy sauce. The prefecture has Japan's highest production and co

foods.name: Karashi renkon (mustard lotus root)
foods.note: Lotus root stuffed with spicy mustard-miso paste, battered and deep-fried. Originated in the Edo era under the Hosokawa clan as a nourishing food.

foods.name: Akaushi (Aka beef / Kumamoto red Wagyu)
foods.note: Red-haired Wagyu raised on the volcanic grasslands around Mt. Aso; lean yet umami-rich, often served as a beef bowl. A registered Geographical Indication produc

foods.name: Taipien (tipien)
foods.note: A glass-noodle soup blending Chinese (Fujian) and Japanese cooking with light chicken broth, vegetables, seafood/pork and a fried egg. Once common across Kyushu

foods.name: Akaushi Beef Street near Aso Shrine (Monzenmachi)
foods.note: A lesser-known lane just beyond Aso Shrine packed with local Akaushi beef eateries, where locals rather than tourists eat the regional red beef.

culture.name: Kumamoto Castle (Kumamoto-jo)
culture.note: One of Japan's three premier castles, completed in 1607 by Kato Kiyomasa; famous for its curved 'musha-gaeshi' stone walls. Now reopened to visitors after 2016

culture.name: Suizenji Jojuen Garden
culture.note: An Edo-period circular stroll garden built by the Hosokawa lords, featuring a spring-fed pond and a miniature Mt. Fuji; a teahouse offers matcha with garden vie

culture.name: Mount Aso
culture.note: One of the world's largest volcanic calderas; a ropeway and viewpoints let visitors approach the active Nakadake crater amid vast grasslands.

culture.name: Kurokawa Onsen
culture.note: A tranquil hot-spring village tucked in the Aso mountains with ~30 traditional ryokan; a rotenburo onsen-hopping pass lets you bathe at outdoor baths across the

culture.name: Kamishikimi Kumanoimasu Shrine
culture.note: A mystical forest shrine in Takamori reached via a moss-covered stone-lantern staircase through towering cedars; the model for the anime film 'Hotarubi no Mori

areas.name: 熊本市
areas.note: Prefectural capital and home to majestic Kumamoto Castle, one of Japan's three famous castles.

areas.name: 阿蘇市
areas.note: Gateway to Mount Aso, featuring one of the world's largest active volcanic calderas and grassland scenery.

areas.name: 天草
areas.note: Bridge-linked island group with UNESCO Hidden Christian sites, dolphin watching, and fresh seafood.

prefectures.name: Oita
prefectures.summary: Oita is widely known as Japan's onsen (hot spring) capital, producing more thermal spring water than any other prefecture, with Beppu's steaming "hells" (jigoku) and its volcanic Kunisaki Peninsula on the Seto Inland Sea.

foods.name: Toriten (chicken tempura)
foods.note: Oita soul food said to have originated in Beppu in the early 1920s: ginger/garlic-seasoned chicken in a light tempura batter, served with ponzu, mustard and a s

foods.name: Dango-jiru (dumpling soup)
foods.note: Hearty Oita farmhouse soup of hand-stretched wheat-flour dumplings simmered with vegetables and miso; a rural staple eaten as a warming, filling meal.

foods.name: Seki-saba / Seki-aji
foods.note: Premium mackerel and horse mackerel raised in the fierce tides of the Bungo Channel; firm-fleshed and prized, often eaten as sashimi.

foods.name: Ryukyu-don
foods.note: A local home-style rice bowl of fresh fish (often aji or mackerel) marinated in soy, sake, mirin, sesame and ginger, served over rice; far less internationally

culture.name: Beppu Jigoku Meguri (Hells of Beppu)
culture.note: A tour of vivid, too-hot-to-bathe thermal springs including the cobalt-blue Umi Jigoku and the blood-red Chinoike Jigoku; Beppu has the largest hot-spring outpu

culture.name: Usuki Stone Buddhas (Usuki Sekibutsu)
culture.note: A group of stone Buddhas carved into rock cliffs over 1,000 years ago; 61 statues are designated National Treasures, set in a park famed for seasonal lotus.

culture.name: Yufuin onsen town & Kinrinko Lake
culture.note: A refined, walkable hot-spring town below Mt. Yufu, known for craft cafes and the misty dawn scenery of Kinrinko Lake.

culture.name: Kunisaki Peninsula & Rokugo Manzan Buddhist culture
culture.note: An off-the-beaten-path region with 1,300+ years of syncretic Buddhist-Shinto mountain worship, ancient temples and sacred trails; far fewer foreign visitors tha

culture.name: Rakanji Temple & Aonodomon (Nakatsu)
culture.note: A cliff-side temple complex whose caves hold over 3,700 stone Buddhist figures, including 500 rakan, near the hand-carved Aonodomon tunnel.

areas.name: 別府
areas.note: Western Japan's largest hot spring resort, famous for the colorful 'hells' (jigoku) and sand baths.

areas.name: 由布院
areas.note: A refined mountain onsen town below Mt. Yufu, known for boutique ryokan and an artsy shopping street.

areas.name: 姫島
areas.note: A volcanic Japan Geopark island off Kunisaki, a rest stop for migrating Asagimadara butterflies in May-June.

prefectures.name: Miyazaki
prefectures.summary: Miyazaki, on Kyushu's sunny southeastern coast, is known for its subtropical Pacific shoreline, surf beaches and palm-lined drives, and for Takachiho Gorge, a mist-filled volcanic ravine tied to Japan's creation myths.

foods.name: Chicken Nanban (チキン南蛮)
foods.note: Miyazaki's signature dish: deep-fried battered chicken dipped in sweet vinegar and topped with tartar sauce. Originated in Nobeoka City in the 1950s; the tartar

foods.name: Jidori no Sumibiyaki (地鶏の炭火焼き)
foods.note: Charcoal-grilled local free-range chicken cut bite-size, seasoned with salt and pepper, and seared over high charcoal heat for a smoky char.

foods.name: Lettuce Maki (レタス巻き)
foods.note: Lesser-known local sushi roll of lettuce, shrimp and a house mayonnaise over sushi rice in seaweed. Invented in 1966 at Ippei Sushi in Miyazaki City and conside

foods.name: Nichinan Katsuo (Nichinan bonito)
foods.note: Nichinan City has one of Japan's largest pole-and-line bonito (katsuo) catches, each fish caught individually by rod. A coastal specialty often overlooked by vi

culture.name: Takachiho Gorge (高千穂峡)
culture.note: V-shaped volcanic gorge carved by the Gokase River, with the 17m Manai Falls. A National Place of Scenic Beauty and Natural Monument; visitors row boats beneath

culture.name: Udo Jingu (鵜戸神宮)
culture.note: Vermilion shrine set inside a seaside cave on a cliff over the Pacific, dedicated to Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto, father of Japan's first emperor. Visitors toss 'un

culture.name: Aoshima Shrine & Devil's Washboard (青島神社・鬼の洗濯板)
culture.note: Shrine on a small subtropical-forested island ringed by the 'Oni no Sentakuita' wave-eroded rock platforms, a National Natural Monument walkable at low tide.

culture.name: Takachiho Yokagura (Night Kagura dance)
culture.note: Sacred Shinto kagura dance dedicated to the gods at Takachiho Shrine, with nightly performances offering an intimate look at Japan's mythological roots away fro

culture.name: Sun Messe Nichinan Moai statues (サンメッセ日南)
culture.note: Hilltop park on the Nichinan Coast with seven full-scale Moai replicas, the only officially Easter-Island-authorized reproductions in the world, overlooking the

areas.name: 宮崎市
areas.note: The prefectural capital and gateway, with palm-lined avenues, beaches and the seaside Aoshima area.

areas.name: 高千穂
areas.note: Mythical town famed for its dramatic Takachiho Gorge, rowboats beneath Manai Falls and Yokagura night dances.

areas.name: 青島
areas.note: Small subtropical island ringed by the wave-cut 'Devil's Washboard' rocks and home to Aoshima Shrine.

prefectures.name: Kagoshima
prefectures.summary: Kagoshima sits at the southern tip of Kyushu beneath Sakurajima, one of Japan's most active volcanoes, which erupts hundreds of times a year across the bay from the city. Beyond its samurai history and hot springs, the prefecture stretches to remote islands including UNESCO-listed Yakushima, famed for its ancient cedar forests.

foods.name: Kurobuta (Berkshire black pork)
foods.note: Kagoshima's signature Berkshire-derived pork, prized for sweet light fat; enjoyed as shabu-shabu hot pot or tonkatsu cutlets.

foods.name: Satsuma imo shochu (sweet-potato distilled spirit)
foods.note: Clear ~25% spirit distilled from local sweet potatoes; Kagoshima has 100+ distilleries producing thousands of varieties.

foods.name: Satsuma-age
foods.note: Deep-fried minced-fish-paste cake, a Kagoshima staple eaten as a snack or side.

foods.name: Kibinago sashimi (silver-stripe round herring)
foods.note: Tiny 10cm fish hand-filleted and arranged in a chrysanthemum 'kikka-zukuri' pattern; spoils fast so rarely sold outside Kagoshima, considered local soul food.

foods.name: Shirokuma (Kagoshima shaved ice)
foods.note: Fluffy shaved ice topped with condensed milk, azuki beans and fruit; far fresher eaten at a Tenmonkan specialty shop than the packaged supermarket version.

culture.name: Sengan-en Garden
culture.note: 1658 Shimadzu-clan villa and garden using active Sakurajima volcano and Kinko Bay as borrowed scenery; part of a UNESCO World Heritage industrial-revolution sit

culture.name: Sakurajima volcano
culture.note: Iconic active volcano facing Kagoshima City, reachable by short ferry; lava trails, hot springs and a visitor center explain its frequent eruptions.

culture.name: Chiran Samurai District
culture.note: Stone-paved street lined with 250-year-old samurai residences and landscaped gardens; often paired with the nearby Chiran Peace Museum on WWII history.

culture.name: Ibusuki sunamushi (volcanic sand bath)
culture.note: 300-year-old wellness ritual where, in a cotton yukata, you are buried up to the neck in naturally hot seaside sand; try Saraku sand-bath center.

culture.name: Kirishima Jingu Shrine
culture.note: 6th-century origin shrine, the largest in southern Kyushu and a noted power spot with an 800-year sacred tree and 'Seven Mysteries' legends.

areas.name: 鹿児島市
areas.note: Prefectural capital and gateway port, with frequent 15-minute ferries crossing Kinko Bay to Sakurajima.

areas.name: 桜島
areas.note: Highly active stratovolcano (formerly an island, now a peninsula joined by lava) that frequently sends ash plumes over the city.

areas.name: 屋久島
areas.note: UNESCO World Natural Heritage island with ancient yakusugi cedars and Kyushu's highest peak, Miyanoura-dake (1,936 m).

prefectures.name: Okinawa
prefectures.summary: Okinawa, Japan's subtropical island chain lying closer to Taiwan than to Tokyo, carries the legacy of the Ryukyu Kingdom centered on Naha and Shuri Castle. It is distinctive for coral reefs, white-sand beaches, and a local cuisine of goya champuru and Okinawa soba, drawing visitors to the Churaumi Aquarium and the outer islands of Ishigaki and Miyako.

foods.name: Goya champuru (ゴーヤーチャンプルー)
foods.note: Okinawa's signature stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork. 'Champuru' means 'something mixed' in the Okinawan dialect; featured by JNTO as a must-try loc

foods.name: Okinawa soba / Soki soba (沖縄そば・ソーキそば)
foods.note: Despite the name, made from wheat (not buckwheat) so closer to udon; served in a savory pork-bonito broth. The 'soki' version is topped with tender braised pork

foods.name: Rafute (ラフテー)
foods.note: Braised pork belly slow-simmered in soy sauce, brown sugar and awamori (local rice spirit) until melt-in-your-mouth tender. A classic of Ryukyu court cuisine.

foods.name: Taco rice (タコライス)
foods.note: Seasoned taco meat, lettuce, cheese and salsa over white rice. A genuinely Okinawan hybrid born from the post-WWII US military presence; emblematic of the islan

foods.name: Blue Seal beni-imo & shikuwasa ice cream (ブルーシール)
foods.note: Founded 1948, slogan 'Born in America, Raised in Okinawa.' Locals favor the uniquely Okinawan flavors: beni-imo (purple sweet potato), shikuwasa (Okinawan lime)

foods.name: Mimigaa & yushi-dofu (ミミガー・ゆし豆腐)
foods.note: Local everyday foods rarely sought by tourists: mimigaa is thinly sliced pig's ear (crunchy, vinegar-dressed) and yushi-dofu is soft unpressed tofu eaten warm.

culture.name: Shuri Castle (Shurijo) / 首里城

culture.name: Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium / 沖縄美ら海水族館
culture.note: One of the world's largest aquariums, anchored by the giant Kuroshio Sea tank where whale sharks and manta rays swim. A flagship Motobu Peninsula attraction.

culture.name: Sefa-Utaki / 斎場御嶽
culture.note: The most sacred utaki (prayer site) of the Ryukyu Kingdom, said to be its place of origin; part of the UNESCO Gusuku Sites listing.

culture.name: Yachimun no Sato pottery village (やちむんの里), Yomitan

culture.name: Nakijin Castle Ruins / 今帰仁城跡
